metaDescription: Six NIIMBOT Bluetooth label printers compared by label width, 300 dpi thermal transfer versus 203 dpi direct thermal, weight and app features.
expertTake: The NIIMBOT M3 is the best of the family for people who need wider labels, because it takes rolls from 20 mm to 78 mm and prints at 300 dpi by thermal transfer. The B1 is the value pick for pantry, craft and shipping stickers, and the D110 is the pocket choice for cables and small jars. Anyone who needs 4x6 shipping labels should skip this brand and buy a desktop roll printer.
introParagraphs: This maker sells a whole ladder of small Bluetooth label printers, from a pocket mini unit to a 3 inch sticker printer, and the names look confusingly similar. Underneath the model letters there are really only a few decisions: label width, resolution and whether the printer uses a ribbon.

Most buyers care about two things after the novelty fades, the cost of label rolls and the reliability of the phone app. Both are worth thinking about before you pick a model, because the printer is only half of what you end up owning.

products.name: NIIMBOT M3 3 inch thermal transfer label printer, 300 dpi
products.description:
The M3 widens the family's reach to 3 inch labels. It takes rolls from 20 mm up to 78 mm wide, so it can make parcel-size address stickers, product labels for boxes and shelf edge labels that the 2 inch models cannot. That range is the main reason it leads this guide.

Resolution is 300 dpi, and it prints by thermal transfer, which uses a ribbon rather than relying on heat-sensitive paper. The listing notes it renders QR codes and small text legibly, and thermal transfer prints are generally more durable than direct thermal ones, so a label on a stored box can last longer. You can edit labels in the app on a phone or on a PC, which helps with larger jobs.

A ribbon-based machine adds a second consumable, so you will buy ribbon and label rolls together and need to match them. Keep the ribbon seated flat, wipe the head occasionally and store rolls dry. If you only need small labels, the B1 will cost less to run.
products.bestFor: Sellers and makers who need wider labels with durable thermal transfer prints.
pros: Takes rolls from 20 to 78 mm wide
300 dpi for sharp QR codes and text
cons: Needs ribbon and label rolls together

products.name: NIIMBOT M2 thermal transfer label maker, 300 dpi, 2 inch

specList.label: Claim
specList.value: Prints last about 10 years without fading

products.description:
Durability is the M2's selling point. It adopts thermal transfer, where a ribbon transfers ink to the label instead of heating coated paper, and the maker claims prints can last about 10 years without fading. Treat that as a marketing claim, but the underlying process is more durable than the direct thermal labels of the D110 and B1.

The listing makes one point very clearly: it is designed only for M2 thermal transfer labels, and standard thermal labels should not be used in it. That means label stock is tied to the maker, which affects cost and availability. With 300 dpi resolution, it produces sharper text and images than the 203 dpi B1.

The M2 suits office and lab labeling where a label must survive, such as sample tubes, equipment tags and archive boxes. Keep spare ribbons, wipe the head as needed and store rolls flat. If durability is not important, the cheaper direct thermal models save money.
products.bestFor: Offices and labs that need labels to stay legible for years.
pros: Suited to office and lab labels
cons: Works only with matching M2 labels
Fade claim is the maker's own

products.name: NIIMBOT B2 portable label maker, 352 g, one-touch printing
products.description:
Offline printing is what the B2 adds. You can press the button on the printer to reprint a stored label without opening the app, which is a real convenience in a bakery or a coffee shop where one label is printed again and again. The printer weighs 352 g, easy to carry in a bag.

It supports label widths from 20 mm to 50 mm and works with white, colored, round and transparent stock, so it handles a wide range of sticker styles. Against the B21 Pro, it trades the 300 dpi and red-black capability for the standalone button. Against the B1, it is similar in width but adds the offline function.

Because the app is still needed for design, the offline feature is best for repeat labels. Keep rolls dry, wipe the head and charge before long sessions. It is a good choice for a counter where one or two labels are printed all day.
products.bestFor: Bakeries and small shops that reprint the same labels all day.
pros: White, colored, round and transparent stock
cons: Sticker rolls are an ongoing cost

products.name: NIIMBOT B1 2 inch Bluetooth label printer, 1500 mAh
products.description:
A middle-of-the-road machine, the B1 handles the standard 50x30 mm sticker. It has a 1500 mAh lithium battery rated for about five hours of work, and it connects to iOS, Android and PC. The listing is upfront about one limitation: it is not compatible with iPad, which matters to tablet users.

It is a direct thermal printer, so labels fade over time, but it is cheaper to run than the thermal transfer M2 and M3. Compared with the D110, it prints on bigger stickers, and compared with the B2, it lacks the offline button. The app is the same family, with a library of fonts, symbols and templates.

Because rolls are a continuing cost, check that your preferred sizes are available. Keep rolls cool, wipe the head if prints weaken and charge before long sessions. It is a sensible all-rounder for home and small shop use.
products.bestFor: Home users and small sellers who want a standard 2 inch sticker printer.
pros: Works with iOS, Android and PC
Direct thermal keeps running cost low

products.name: NIIMBOT B21 Pro 300 dpi red and black label maker
products.description:
Red and black on one label is the headline here, and it comes at 300 dpi. A printable width of 48 mm across labels from 20 to 50 mm gives room for a colored warning stripe plus normal text. For an office that wants to highlight expiry dates or priority items, the extra color is useful.

Automatic label identification reads the loaded roll and tells the app the size, which prevents the classic mistake of designing for the wrong sticker. The app offers a long list of fonts and languages and over a hundred borders. Compared with the M2, this model brings color while the M2 brings the ribbon durability claim.

Two-color labels need the matching stock, so plan for that cost. Keep the rolls sealed, wipe the head and charge the battery before a long job. It is a good fit for a small office that wants a pop of color.
products.bestFor: Offices that want red highlights on labels at 300 dpi.
pros: Red and black printing at 300 dpi

products.name: NIIMBOT D110 mini label maker with three label rolls
products.description:
Smallness is the entire pitch of the D110. At 149 g it is the lightest printer in this guide, and it handles labels up to 15 mm wide, such as 12x40 mm cable flags and spice jar labels. The upgraded version adds an automatic rewind, so the position of the first label is set without wasting one.

The bundle includes three rolls in different colors, which gives a quick start. It is a direct thermal printer at 203 dpi, like the B1, so labels fade with heat. Compared with the M3 and B2, it does not do wide labels, and compared with the P21 style handhelds, it works with sticker rolls.

Keep rolls in a bag, wipe the head if prints dim and charge before a session. It is the easiest to carry and the simplest to use of the family.
products.bestFor: People who want a pocket printer for cables, jars and small items.
pros: Automatic rewind saves the first label
Three colored rolls in the bundle

buyingCriteria.explanation: The D110 stops at 15 mm, the B1, B2 and B21 Pro handle roughly 20 to 50 mm and the M3 reaches 78 mm. Choose the width for your largest label. Most pantry and craft labels fit within 50 mm, but box and address labels need more. Measure the surface you are labeling, because a label that wraps a corner or a curved lid needs more room than the same label on a flat bin. Also remember the printable area is slightly narrower than the roll, so a 50 mm roll prints about 48 mm of image, and a design built edge to edge will lose its border.

The M2 and M3 use thermal transfer with a ribbon, producing more durable prints at 300 dpi. The B1 and D110 use direct thermal at 203 dpi, which is cheaper but fades. Decide whether the label must last years. A pantry sticker replaced every season does not need a ribbon, but an archive box, a sample tube or a tool tag that is rarely touched is exactly where a faded direct thermal label becomes a problem. The extra cost of the ribbon is small next to relabeling a shelf.

The M2, M3 and B21 Pro print at 300 dpi, while the B1 and D110 print at 203 dpi. 300 dpi helps QR codes and small text. For large text and simple icons, 203 dpi is enough. Where 300 dpi really shows is on QR codes under about 20 mm square and on type smaller than about 6 point, where the extra dots keep the edges crisp. If your labels are mostly names and dates in bold type, the cheaper 203 dpi models give the same visible result.

The M2 works only with its own thermal transfer labels, and other models use the maker's rolls. That limits supplier choice. Check which rolls the printer accepts and how easy they are to buy. Matched stock is how these brands keep their margins, so a printer that looks cheap can be expensive to feed over a year. Add up the cost of a few hundred labels before you decide, and see whether more than one seller carries the size you need.

The B1 supports iOS, Android and PC but not iPad. The M3 edits on mobile and PC. A printer that works with your device matters more than any spec. Tablet owners in particular should read the compatibility line closely, since a model that works on phones may not run on the same app on a tablet. Check that the app is available in your country's store and ask whether it needs an account.

The D110 weighs 149 g, and the B2 weighs 352 g with offline reprinting. A counter that prints the same label repeatedly benefits from an offline button. A desk printer does not. Weight also decides where a printer lives: a 149 g mini rides in a pocket, while a heavier unit stays at the counter. If you carry it to markets or classrooms, a smaller battery that charges by USB is easier to live with than a bigger machine.

specDecoder.meaning: About 12 dots per millimeter, finer than the 203 dpi of entry units. It sharpens small text and QR codes.
specDecoder.watchFor: The M2, M3 and B21 Pro list it.

specDecoder.meaning: A ribbon transfers ink onto the label. The result is more durable than heat on coated paper.
specDecoder.watchFor: The M2 and M3 use it, with matching labels.

specDecoder.meaning: Battery capacity in milliamp-hours. A larger number means longer use between charges.
specDecoder.watchFor: The B1 lists 1500 mAh and about five hours of work.

specDecoder.meaning: The width the head actually prints, which is less than the stated label width.
specDecoder.watchFor: The B21 Pro lists 48 mm for 50 mm labels.

specDecoder.meaning: A button on the printer reprints a saved label without the app.

howWeEvaluated.title: Width range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared label width ranges from 15 mm on the D110 to 78 mm on the M3. Width was the first filter. We judged how each printer matches common sticker sizes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Print method
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated thermal transfer from direct thermal and noted the dpi of each. The M2 and M3 lead on durability, and the B1 and D110 lead on running cost. We treated durability claims as the maker's.

howWeEvaluated.title: App and platform
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked supported platforms and noted that the B1 does not work with iPad. App libraries were compared. A printer that fits your phone was valued over a longer feature list.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weights, from 149 g on the D110 to 352 g on the B2. Battery claims were noted. Offline use was treated as a counter feature.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership reality
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on owner feedback patterns, we weighed label roll supply, ribbon cost and app updates. A printer tied to matched stock earned less flexibility. We did not quote prices. Since the family shares one app, we also considered how well each model fits the same workflow, so an owner could move up the range without relearning the software.

cards.label: Thermal transfer
cards.text: The M2 and M3 use a ribbon at 300 dpi. Prints last longer and read sharper. They need ribbon and matched labels.

cards.label: Direct thermal
cards.text: The B1, B2, B21 Pro and D110 use heat on coated paper. They are cheaper to run. Labels fade in heat and sun.

howToChoose.note: Choose transfer for archive and lab labels; choose direct for pantry and shop labels.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A label size that matches your packaging, labels that stick to your containers and an easy way to reprint a standard label.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The B2 suits a counter, the M3 suits box labels, and the B1 suits shelf stickers.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You need durable labels or wide rolls. The M3 and M2 are worth it.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You label small items occasionally. The D110 or B1 is enough.

maintenance.why: Dust and residue cut contrast. Use alcohol on a swab.
A wrinkled ribbon prints streaks on the M2 and M3. A crooked roll jams the feed.
A low pack causes light prints. Charge fully before big jobs.
Heat darkens thermal paper. Keep spares in their bags.
Pairing depends on current software. Outdated versions can lose the Bluetooth link.

faq.q: Which NIIMBOT is best for shipping labels?
faq.a: None prints full 4x6 labels. The M3 reaches 78 mm, which suits box and address labels.

faq.q: Is thermal transfer worth the cost?
faq.a: Yes for labels that must last. The M2 and M3 print at 300 dpi with a ribbon.

faq.q: Does the B1 work with iPad?
faq.a: No, the listing says it is incompatible with iPad. It supports iOS phones, Android and PC.

faq.q: Can I use any label rolls?
faq.a: The M2 works only with its own thermal transfer labels. Other models also prefer the maker's rolls.

faq.q: How long does the battery last?
faq.a: The B1 lists about five hours of work from its 1500 mAh pack. Use and temperature change it.
Direct thermal labels fade over time. Thermal transfer labels last longer.
